help: import:
usage: poisson-trace import [-h] [--version] [--plain] TOOL ...

Read the result files another tool already wrote and write them as one new run of a store in
Prove's format, for Poisson Trace's verbs to read. One import is one version: import the old
version and the new one into the same store, then compare them with poisson-trace fix-check.
A store is the folder Prove keeps runs in; a case is one test case or question of the tool's
files, and the rows that share a case are its repeats.

A folder of results may be given in place of the files, and in place of the tool too
(poisson-trace import ./results --store trace-store): its files are found by the readers'
own detectors and read as one run, named after the folder unless --run names it.

options:
  -h, --help      show this help message and exit
  --version       print the versions of Trace, Prove and Python
  --plain         print plain text with no colour, as on a pipe; may come
                  before or after the tool

tools:
  TOOL
    deepeval      DeepEval's saved test runs, as DeepEval 4.2.6 writes them.
    ragas         Ragas's per-row score tables, saved as CSV, JSON Lines, JSON
                  or Parquet.
    table         Any table of results a tool or a script saved: CSV, JSON
                  Lines, JSON or Parquet.
    junit         JUnit XML reports, as pytest, Jest, Go, Maven and CI systems
                  write them.
    promptfoo     promptfoo results, as ``promptfoo eval -o results.json`` (or
                  ``.jsonl``) writes them.
    inspect       Inspect AI logs: the ``.eval`` archive, the ``.json`` log,
                  and an unpacked ``.eval`` folder.
    openai-evals  OpenAI Evals records, as ``oaieval ... --record_path
                  log.jsonl`` writes them.

examples:
  poisson-trace import deepeval results/test_run_20260905_185407.json \
      --store trace-store --run before --metric "Tests Passed" --cut recorded --case name
  poisson-trace import ragas base-scores.jsonl --store trace-store --run base \
      --metric faithfulness --cut 0.5 --below --case-column question_id
  poisson-trace import table results-old.csv --store trace-store --run old \
      --case-column case --outcome-column outcome --failed failed --failed crashed
  poisson-trace import junit reports/old.xml --store trace-store --run old
  poisson-trace import promptfoo results.json --store trace-store --run old --prompt 1 --case var:case
  poisson-trace import inspect logs/old.eval --store trace-store --run old
  poisson-trace import openai-evals old.jsonl --store trace-store --run old

app.verdict compare:
poisson-trace · compare  agent before → agent after                                                           trace.toml
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  different  failures come later after the change

  Compared  before agent before against after agent after, on the same 4 inputs: 160 tries each. A try counts as failed
            when it ended timeout or violated.
  Question  Step by step, among tries still going, did the after version fail more or less often? You asked to see that
            rate change 1.5-fold, either way.
  Answer    Failures come later. 41 of 160 tries failed after and 72 of 160 before; if each input failed equally often
            under both versions, a gap at least this big, either way, would turn up less than once in 1,000 (counting
            tries as independent); after against before, the per-step failure rate is 0.22 times as high (0.14 to 0.35).
  Next      Compare how often each version fails overall: `poisson-trace fix-check "agent before" "agent after" --inputs
            all --max-mde X`, choosing X before you look.
  next  poisson-trace fix-check "agent before" "agent after" --inputs all

  before you act on this
  - They started 2 s apart. Trace can't tell whether they were run side by side, so anything else that changed between
    them (the provider, the model behind the API, the day) may be part of the difference, in either direction.
  - Both runs name the same target (mock-agent); Trace can't tell what differs between them, only what you tell it.
  - A try that finished without failing counts as still going up to its last step, so this mixes how often and how early
    tries fail. Tries of the same input are counted as separate chances; if they are near copies, this is more confident
    than it should be.

app.verdict fix-check:
poisson-trace · fix-check  agent before → agent after                                                         trace.toml
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  different  the new version failed less often

  Compared  old agent before against new agent after, on the same 4 inputs: 160 tries of each. A try counts as failed
            when it ended timeout or violated.
  Question  Did the new version fail more or less often than the old? You asked that the run be able to catch a 10-point
            drop in how often it fails.
  Answer    Fewer failures, if tries of an input count as independent (here they are fairly alike). The new version
            failed 41 of 160 tries and the old 72 of 160 (19 fewer per 100 tries); 31 of the net 31 fewer failures come
            from task_id search at tool_fail_rate 0.55 and task_id refund at tool_fail_rate 0.55.
  Next      Run both versions side by side on these inputs with your own harness, then run `poisson-trace fix-check` on
            the two new runs.
  next  poisson-trace fix-check --help

  before you act on this
  - They started 2 s apart. Trace can't tell whether they were run side by side, so anything else that changed between
    them (the provider, the model behind the API, the day) may be part of the difference, in either direction.
  - Both runs name the same target (mock-agent); Trace can't tell what differs between them, only what you tell it.
  - These results fit anything from 12 to 27 fewer failures per 100 tries, but that range is only a rough guide here and
    may be off either way (fewer than 10 inputs vary): don't use it to rule sizes in or out.
  - Tries of the same input are counted as separate chances; here they are fairly alike (agreement 0.61, where 0 is no
    more alike than chance and 1 is identical), and if they are near copies the answer is more confident than it should
    be.
  - If each input failed equally often under both versions, a gap at least this big, either way, would turn up less than
    once in 1,000 (counting tries as independent).
  - A check of which inputs went up and which went down can't rule out chance on its own (p = 0.500 in the report), so
    the gap rests on task_id refund at tool_fail_rate 0.55 and task_id search at tool_fail_rate 0.55. Without task_id
    refund at tool_fail_rate 0.55 and task_id search at tool_fail_rate 0.55, the gap is 0.00 points (p = 1.00).
  - Before putting the difference down to the version, run both side by side.

app.could not say:
poisson-trace · could not say  agent before → agent after                                                     trace.toml
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - The step index is where the run stopped, not why. A run that died at a tool step may have gone wrong three steps
    earlier.
  - Capped runs are censored at their last recorded step. If they would have died soon after, the curve is optimistic by
    that much. A run that timed out ends where it stopped, counted beside the kinds and not as a death; the header
    counts both.
  - Excluded rows are not on the curve; the header counts them by reason.
  - On one run, this is a description. Only a comparison of two stored runs on the same cells says whether anything
    moved, and only within what it could not have detected.
  next  poisson-trace fix-check "agent before" "agent after" --inputs all
